blocks.eyebrow: Chapter 2 - Making a ledger out of it
blocks.heading: What the signature covers
text: Caleb's transaction leaves his laptop and passes through a dozen strangers' machines before any miner sees it.
Every one of them can read it. Whether any of them can rewrite it comes down to a single byte.

blocks.heading: The digest is a copy of the transaction
text: Signing does not hash "the transaction" as broadcast. It hashes a specially built copy of it.
A flag byte, carried alongside the signature, decides what goes into that copy.

blocks.alt: Three panels comparing sighash flags: ALL signs inputs and outputs, NONE leaves outputs open, SINGLE signs one output only
blocks.caption: Same signature algorithm, three different promises about what may still change.

blocks.heading: What Caleb's wallet uses
text: `SIGHASH_ALL`, value `0x01`, the default since the beginning. It commits to every input and every output.
Move one satoshi of the 0.0309 change to a different address and the signature stops verifying. Nora's 0.05 is nailed down by the same byte.

blocks.heading: The alternative is a blank cheque
text: `SIGHASH_NONE` signs the inputs and _no outputs at all_. The signature is valid no matter where the money goes.
Hand that to the network and the first node to receive it can point 0.0812 BTC at itself.

blocks.question: That sounds indefensible. Why does the flag exist at all?
answer: Because sometimes an incomplete transaction is the point. `SIGHASH_SINGLE` combined with `ANYONECANPAY` signs one input and one output and leaves the rest open - which is exactly "I will sell this thing for that price, somebody fill in the rest".
Atomic swaps and offer protocols are built from it. The flag is not a weakness; using the wrong one is.

blocks.heading: A signature cannot contain itself
text: The signature ends up inside the transaction, so it cannot be part of what it signs.
The resolution is blunt: before hashing, every input's script field is emptied, and the one being signed is filled with the locking script of the output it spends.

blocks.heading: The digest that was a constant
text: `SIGHASH_SINGLE` signs the output at the same index as the input. If input 3 exists and there are only two outputs, there is nothing to sign.
Legacy hashing did not reject that. It returned the digest `0x00...01` - a fixed value, identical for every transaction.
A signature over a constant commits to nothing, and can be lifted and replayed elsewhere.

blocks.heading: What BIP-143 fixed
text: Segwit brought a new digest algorithm. It removes the constant-digest case, and it commits to **the value of the input being spent** - which legacy hashing never did.

blocks.question: Why would a signer need the input's amount committed, when it already commits to every output?
answer: Because the fee is the difference, and the input amounts are not in the transaction - they live in the outputs being spent.

A hardware wallet shown false input values would compute a false fee. It could be told it was sending 0.0812 with a 0.0003 fee while actually authorising almost all of it to the miner. BIP-143 makes that lie invalid.

blocks.heading: It also stopped a quadratic
text: Legacy hashing re-serialised the whole transaction once per input, so signing cost grew with the square of the input count.
BIP-143 precomputes the shared parts. One large transaction could previously force every node in the world to do minutes of hashing.

blocks.heading: The edge of what a signature can do

text: Even `SIGHASH_ALL` covers only this transaction. It says nothing about **when** it happens, **which block** it lands in, or what happens if Caleb signs a second transaction spending the same 0.0812 coin.
Both would verify perfectly. Cryptography has run out of things to say.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: A signature is only as strong as the scope it commits to, and the scope is a design decision, not a mathematical fact.
Nora's phone is about to be told the payment arrived. It holds none of the chain, and it is going to check anyway.
